# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 79 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 79 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_079_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 8 — The Branches Interpreted

**1** Among those with green branches, the angel ordered crowns to be brought — crowns woven from palm branches — and he crowned those who had returned completely green branches and led them into the tower. **2** Those whose branches were green but cracked were also sent into the tower, and they were given seals. **3** Everyone who entered the tower was dressed identically — in garments white as snow. **4** He also sent in those who had returned branches half-green and half-withered, giving them clothing and seals. **5** But those who returned branches dried out and worm-eaten — these were apostates: people who had betrayed the community of faith, blasphemed the Lord through wicked actions, and were ashamed to be identified by his name. They were completely lost. **6** Those whose branches were dried out but not worm-eaten had been hearers of God's word but kept on sinning without turning back. Those who returned branches half-green and half-withered were people absorbed in business who never connected closely with other believers — so they were half-alive and half-dead spiritually. **7** Those who returned branches two-thirds green and one-third withered were people who had repeatedly denied their faith under pressure. **8** Those who returned branches two-thirds withered and one-third green were believers who had largely lived in sin and wrongdoing — yet a remnant of integrity remained in them. **9** Those who returned nearly all-green branches with only the very tip dried out — these were truly faithful believers with only minor faults. **10** Those whose branches were completely dried out had already walked away from the faith and would not repent — their hearts had hardened beyond reach. The Spirit of the Lord had left them.

---

*PNEUMA translates the theological categories into contemporary spiritual language while preserving the structure of Hermas's ten-class typology.*
